old_entry.title: The ruler of Lagash has to decide
old_entry.summary: Addis shaped an economic simulation around a pupil’s changing responsibilities.
body: The 1967 project report names Mabel Addis as writer of the Sumerian Game’s instructional version and IBM’s William McKay as programmer. Its starting point was a classroom problem, not a shop shelf: children would make decisions inside a model of an ancient economy. Addis’s work supplied the situation in which those calculations would mean something. The student became Luduga, ruler of Lagash, receiving reports and deciding what to do. Writing and programming were distinct contributions to the same experience, and the contemporary report makes both names recoverable.

After an earlier group played, Addis revised the game during summer 1966. The report describes shorter, less repetitive messages and a clearer connection between economic concepts and the script. Recorded discussions among advisers broke up the reading, while charts and other visuals were made more useful to the lesson. Later stages were also reorganized to move routine calculations to the computer. The revision changed what demanded attention, giving the human more room to concentrate on the decisions the exercise was meant to teach.

The Strong’s collection contains three long teletype printouts, 39 introductory slides and the research report. A printout is a revealing survival. Instead of a screenshot of a recovered program, it records messages, responses and the changing state of a particular session. Slides preserve another part of the teaching arrangement, outside the terminal itself. The game therefore cannot be understood only as words generated by a computer. Its surviving materials show a coordinated lesson spread across paper, projected images and a pupil waiting to receive the next report.

The papers reached The Strong through donations from Devin Monnens and Alexandra Johnson; the museum subsequently added a copy of the research report. Its finding aid identifies access conditions for reference scans of the printouts. Research access is not the same as permission to redistribute each item. These limits belong to the story of what survives. The collection makes the instructional work of Addis and her collaborators visible while leaving gaps that a museum should describe, rather than fill with an invented reconstruction.

In 2023, the Game Developers Choice Awards selected Addis for its posthumous Pioneer Award. The organizers highlighted the narrated decisions and the slides accompanied by synchronized sound in The Sumerian Game. Addis drew on her training in ancient history at Barnard College while working as a grade-school teacher. Her classroom project brings together subject knowledge, writing and computer simulation around the choices of a pupil.
